lines.speaker: Cnemon
lines.text: Well. This is exactly what the proverb says: the fawn swallowed the lion.
lines.note: The proverb reverses the expected predator/prey relationship — the hunter became the hunted. Cnemon delivers it with the flat exhaustion of a man who has just understood the joke at his own expense.

lines.speaker: Damasias
lines.text: What are you so worked up about, Cnemon?

lines.speaker: Cnemon
lines.text: What am I worked up about? I've been outwitted, that's what. I left an heir I never intended to leave — the one person I would have done anything to cut out — and he's got everything.

lines.speaker: Cnemon
lines.text: There was a man — Hermolaus, very wealthy, no children — and I was cultivating him, with an eye to the inheritance. He didn't seem to mind the attention. So I came up with what I thought was a rather clever move: I had my own will drawn up and made sure he heard about it. Left him everything I had — the idea being that he'd take the hint and return the favour.

lines.speaker: Cnemon
lines.text: What he put in his own will, I have no idea. I never found out — my roof fell on me and I died on the spot. And now Hermolaus has everything I owned. Like a sea-bass that swallows the bait and takes the hook down with it.

lines.speaker: Damasias
lines.text: Not just the hook — he swallowed the fisherman too. You set a trap and sprung it on yourself.

lines.speaker: Cnemon
lines.text: So it appears. [pause] Hence the weeping.
lines.note: Delivered completely deadpan, after a beat. The laugh is in the understatement.
